entries.meaning: Make an idea land — to say it in a way the other person actually takes in.
examples: She never quite gets her ideas across in meetings.
He got across the danger in three sentences.
I don't think the joke got across.
Try a diagram if the numbers won't get the point across.
I said it twice and still couldn't get it across.
The ad gets across one message and one only.
entries.pronunciation note: across is an adverb particle here, so it takes the stress — get it aCROSS, never GET it across
entries.separable: yes — get your point across or get across your point, and with a pronoun the object must split: get it across, never ✗ get across it.
entries.transitive: either — usually takes an object (get the idea across), but the message itself can be the subject: the warning got across.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and causative: you cause an idea to land (she gets her ideas across in meetings), and the progressive is normal — I'm still not getting it across. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: restricted. Causative get fights the passive even where there is an object: the point was finally gotten across is possible but stiff, and Americans say the point finally got across instead. The object-less the joke got across has no passive at all.
entries.see also: get through to, get at, get over

entries.meaning: Keep at somebody until they do the thing; or, of a job, attack it with energy.
examples: You need to get after him about that permission slip.
My mother got after me for weeks until I called the dentist.
Somebody should get after the landlord about the heat.
Practice starts at six, so let's get after it.
They came out after halftime and really got after it.

senses.head: Nag somebody into acting
body: American and informal, usually with about or to do. You get after a person, not after a task. (подгонять, дёргать)
examples: You need to get after him about that permission slip.
My mother got after me for weeks until I called the dentist.
Somebody should get after the landlord about the heat.

senses.head: get after it — throw yourself into the work
body: A fixed American expression, at home in gyms, locker rooms, and job sites. (поднажать, взяться за дело)
examples: Practice starts at six, so let's get after it.
They came out after halftime and really got after it.

entries.pronunciation note: after is a preposition, so the verb keeps the main stress — GET after him
entries.русский: подгонять, дёргать (чтобы сделал); взяться за дело
entries.separable: no — the object follows the whole phrase: get after your brother. ✗ get your brother after, ✗ get him after.
entries.register: informal — very common in American speech, rare in writing
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, nagging a person (my mother got after me for weeks) and attacking a job (let's get after it); the progressive is at home in each — somebody's getting after the landlord about the heat.
entries.passive: no. ✗ the landlord was gotten after about the heat is not English, and get after it is a frozen idiom with nothing to promote: ✗ it was gotten after.
entries.see also: get on with, get at, go at

entries.meaning: Make progress — rise at work, or climb out from under what you owe.
examples: You can't get ahead at that company without a degree.
She works two jobs just to get ahead.
Nobody gets ahead by keeping quiet in meetings.
Let's not get ahead of ourselves.
Two of our rivals have gotten ahead of us on price.
We got ahead of the story by announcing it ourselves.

senses.head: Do well, move up
body: The career and money sense, often with in or a bare get ahead. (продвигаться, преуспевать)
examples: You can't get ahead at that company without a degree.
She works two jobs just to get ahead.
Nobody gets ahead by keeping quiet in meetings.

senses.head: get ahead of — outpace or anticipate
body: With of, either beating a rival or jumping too far forward in an argument. (опережать, забегать вперёд)
examples: Let's not get ahead of ourselves.
Two of our rivals have gotten ahead of us on price.
We got ahead of the story by announcing it ourselves.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress — get aHEAD
entries.separable: not applicable — get ahead has no object to place. A target arrives through of: get ahead of the competition, never ✗ get the competition ahead.
entries.transitive: no — intransitive; get ahead of takes its object through the preposition
entries.verb type: action — dynamic. Both the rise at work sense (she works two jobs just to get ahead) and get ahead of (we got ahead of the story) describe progress being made, not a state held.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so there is no object to promote, and the prepositional passive fails too: ✗ we were gotten ahead of on price, ✗ ourselves shouldn't be gotten ahead of.
entries.see also: get by, get on, get through

entries.meaning: Have a friendly relationship with somebody; also, manage well enough with what you have.
examples: The two of them get along fine now.
I never got along with my first boss.
They have gotten along much better since the move.
She gets along on very little money.
How is your father getting along after the surgery?
It's late — I should be getting along.

senses.head: Have a good relationship
body: The main American sense. The other person comes in after with. (ладить, уживаться)
examples: The two of them get along fine now.
I never got along with my first boss.
They have gotten along much better since the move.

senses.head: Manage, cope
body: Usually with on or without, about money, health, or age. (справляться, обходиться)
examples: She gets along on very little money.
How is your father getting along after the surgery?

senses.head: Be on your way
body: Dated in America, and always in the progressive: I should be getting along. (отправляться, идти)
examples: It's late — I should be getting along.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — get aLONG
entries.separable: not applicable — no object. The other person arrives through with: get along with my sister, never ✗ get my sister along.
entries.register: everyday — the standard American choice; British English prefers get on with
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, though the be friendly sense names a relationship that holds over time; the progressive still works (they've been getting along better since the move), and the be on your way sense lives only there: I should be getting along.
entries.passive: no — intransitive in all three senses. The other person arrives through with, never as an object: ✗ my first boss was never gotten along with.
entries.see also: get on with, get by, get on

entries.meaning: Move about from place to place; find a way past something in your way; or, of news, spread.
examples: He gets around town on an old bicycle.
Since the hip replacement she gets around with a cane.
There is no getting around the paperwork.
Their lawyers found a way to get around the ban.
Word got around fast.
It got around that he was leaving.

senses.head: Move about, travel
body: About mobility rather than distance: how a person navigates a town or a house. (передвигаться)
examples: He gets around town on an old bicycle.
Since the hip replacement she gets around with a cane.

senses.head: Evade something standing in your way
body: Rules, laws, and paperwork are the usual objects. (обходить (закон, правило))
examples: There is no getting around the paperwork.
Their lawyers found a way to get around the ban.

senses.head: Spread, of news
body: The subject is word, it, or a rumor; no object at all. (распространяться, расходиться)
examples: Word got around fast.
It got around that he was leaving.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — get aROUND
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle); prepositional when an obstacle follows
entries.separable: no — when there is an object it follows the whole phrase: get around the rules, never ✗ get the rules around.
entries.transitive: either — no object in the travel and rumor senses, an object in the evasion sense
entries.register: everyday — British English says get round
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: moving about (he gets around town on an old bicycle), evading (their lawyers found a way to get around the ban), and spreading (word got around fast).
entries.passive: restricted. Only the evasion sense has an object, and even there the passive is stiff: the ban was gotten around by their lawyers is possible, but their lawyers got around the ban is what people actually say. ✗ town is gotten around by bicycle.
entries.see also: get around to, get out of, go around

entries.meaning: Finally do the thing you have been putting off.
examples: I finally got around to fixing the fence.
She never got around to answering my email.
We'll get around to it eventually.
He has been meaning to call, but he hasn't gotten around to it.
If I get around to the attic this weekend, I'll look for the box.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle around carries the stress and to stays weak — get aROUND tuh
entries.separable: no — the object follows the whole phrase, pronoun and all: get around to the dishes, get around to it. ✗ get the dishes around to, ✗ get around the dishes to. (Nearly every three-part verb behaves this way; get over with, below, is the one exception on this page.)
entries.transitive: yes — the object is usually an -ing form
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; it names the moment a long-postponed action finally starts (I finally got around to fixing the fence), usually with an -ing form.
entries.passive: no. The three-part verb refuses it: ✗ the fence was finally gotten around to, ✗ my email was never gotten around to.
entries.see also: get down to, get to, put off

entries.meaning: Reach something hard to reach, or drive at a point, or keep picking at a person.
examples: I can't get at the shelf without a ladder.
The raccoons got at the trash again.
What exactly are you getting at?
I couldn't tell what she was getting at.
He feels like his manager is always getting at him.
Somebody had gotten at the witness before the trial.

senses.head: Reach, gain access to
body: Physical or informational: a high shelf, a locked file, the facts. (добраться до, достать)
examples: I can't get at the shelf without a ladder.
The raccoons got at the trash again.

senses.head: Be driving at, imply
body: Almost always in a question or a negative, and usually in the progressive. (клонить к, иметь в виду)
examples: What exactly are you getting at?
I couldn't tell what she was getting at.

senses.head: Keep criticizing somebody
body: Informal, and always about a person. (придираться к, доставать)
examples: He feels like his manager is always getting at him.

senses.head: Tamper with, reach corruptly
body: Of witnesses, juries, and officials — someone has bribed or threatened them. (подкупить, повлиять на)
examples: Somebody had gotten at the witness before the trial.

entries.pronunciation note: at is a preposition and normally reduces to /ət/, with the stress on the verb — though it takes the stress when it ends a question: What are you getting AT?
entries.русский: добраться до; клонить к; придираться к
entries.separable: no — get at the truth, never ✗ get the truth at.
entries.register: everyday — the criticizing sense is informal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the reach, criticize, and tamper senses (the raccoons got at the trash, his manager is always getting at him). The be driving at sense is a verb of meaning and lives almost entirely in the progressive: what are you getting at?
entries.passive: restricted. The tamper sense passivizes naturally — the witness had been gotten at before the trial. Elsewhere it is marginal or impossible: the shelf can't be gotten at without a ladder is stiff, and ✗ what was being gotten at? fails outright.
entries.see also: get to, get through to, get after

entries.meaning: Escape, or simply manage to leave — including leaving town for a break.
examples: Two of them got away before the police arrived.
The dog got away from the sitter on Tuesday.
I couldn't get away from the office until eight.
We're trying to get away for a few days in October.
There's no getting away from the fact that we're two months late.

senses.head: Escape
body: Of suspects, animals, and anything that slips your grip. (сбежать, скрыться)
examples: Two of them got away before the police arrived.
The dog got away from the sitter on Tuesday.

senses.head: Manage to leave; take a break
body: Often about work you cannot walk out of, or a short vacation. (вырваться, уехать)
examples: I couldn't get away from the office until eight.
We're trying to get away for a few days in October.

senses.head: there's no getting away from — you cannot dodge the fact
body: A fixed frame introducing something inconvenient and true. (от этого никуда не деться)
examples: There's no getting away from the fact that we're two months late.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — get aWAY
entries.separable: not applicable — get away itself takes no object, and what you escape arrives through from: get away from the office, get away from it. ✗ get the office away. (Moving somebody else out of danger is the causative get the kids away from the window, where the object belongs to get — a different pattern.)
entries.verb type: action — dynamic verb of escape and departure (two of them got away, we're trying to get away for a few days). The fixed there's no getting away from the fact presents a truth rather than a movement.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; what you escape arrives through from, and the prepositional passive fails: ✗ the office couldn't be gotten away from until eight.
entries.see also: get away with, get out, get off

entries.meaning: Do something wrong and go unpunished.
examples: He got away with it because nobody checked the receipts.
You won't get away with lying to her twice.
They have gotten away with far worse than this.
Kids will get away with whatever you let them.
I got away with wearing jeans to the interview.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle away takes the stress and with stays weak — get aWAY with
entries.separable: no — the object follows the whole phrase, pronoun and all: get away with murder, get away with it. ✗ get murder away with, ✗ get away murder with.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: doing something wrong and escaping the consequence (he got away with it because nobody checked the receipts).
entries.passive: no. Despite the obligatory object, the three-part verb has no passive: ✗ murder is gotten away with every day, ✗ lying to her twice won't be gotten away with.
entries.see also: get off, get out of, get by

entries.meaning: Return from somewhere; or get something back into your hands.
examples: We got back from Denver on Sunday.
Call me when you get back.
She never got her books back.
I finally got it back after three emails.
He got back every dollar he put in.
Get back — that wire is live.

senses.head: Return, come home
body: No object; the place arrives through from or to. (вернуться, возвратиться)
examples: We got back from Denver on Sunday.
Call me when you get back.

senses.head: Recover something lost or lent
body: Here the object can sit on either side of back, and a pronoun must sit in front of it. (вернуть себе, получить обратно)
examples: She never got her books back.
I finally got it back after three emails.
He got back every dollar he put in.

senses.head: Move away — imperative
body: A shouted warning: step back from something dangerous. (отойди, назад)
examples: Get back — that wire is live.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — get BACK
entries.separable: yes in the recover sense — get your deposit back or get back your deposit, and a pronoun must split: get it back, never ✗ get back it. In the return home sense there is no object at all.
entries.transitive: either — no object when it means return, an object when it means recover
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: returning (call me when you get back), recovering something (she never got her books back), and the shouted imperative get back — that wire is live.
entries.passive: no in practice. The recover sense is causative get, which blocks it: ✗ her books were never gotten back, ✗ every dollar was gotten back. English keeps the active — he got back every dollar he put in.
entries.see also: get back at, get back to, give back

entries.meaning: Do something to hurt somebody who hurt you first.
examples: She spread the story to get back at her ex.
He's just trying to get back at me for the parking thing.
Don't post anything to get back at them; it always backfires.
They got back at the coach by refusing to play the second half.
There's no point getting back at people who have already moved on.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle back carries the stress — get BACK at him
entries.separable: no — the person follows the whole phrase: get back at your brother, ✗ get your brother back at, ✗ get him back at.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic verb of revenge (she spread the story to get back at her ex), often in the progressive: he's just trying to get back at me.
entries.passive: no. ✗ her ex was gotten back at, ✗ the coach was gotten back at by the players — the pattern has no passive despite always taking an object.
entries.see also: get back, get off, go after

entries.meaning: Answer somebody later; or return to a task or a subject you left.
examples: Let me check the calendar and get back to you.
Nobody ever got back to me about the refund.
I should get back to work.
We'll get back to that question at the end.
It took her a month to get back to running.

senses.head: Reply later
body: The standard American way to promise an answer you do not have yet. (связаться позже, ответить)
examples: Let me check the calendar and get back to you.
Nobody ever got back to me about the refund.

senses.head: Return to a task or a topic
body: The object is the work, the subject, or the routine you had stepped away from. (вернуться к)
examples: I should get back to work.
We'll get back to that question at the end.
It took her a month to get back to running.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle back carries the stress and to stays weak — get BACK tuh you
entries.separable: no — get back to the customer, ✗ get the customer back to, ✗ get back the customer to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, promising a later answer (let me check the calendar and get back to you) and resuming a task or topic (I should get back to work).
entries.passive: no. ✗ I was never gotten back to about the refund, ✗ that question will be gotten back to at the end.
entries.see also: get back, get around to, get down to

entries.meaning: Fall behind where you should be; or throw your weight behind somebody.
examples: We got behind on the rent in March.
Two rainy weeks and the whole crew got behind.
The union got behind the proposal.
Once the mayor got behind it, the money appeared.
If everyone gets behind her, she can win the seat.

senses.head: Fall behind schedule or payments
body: No object, usually with on or with. (отставать, запаздывать)
examples: We got behind on the rent in March.
Two rainy weeks and the whole crew got behind.

senses.head: Support, back
body: The American idiom for public, active support — of a candidate, a bill, a plan. (поддержать, встать за)
examples: The union got behind the proposal.
Once the mayor got behind it, the money appeared.
If everyone gets behind her, she can win the seat.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on behind — get beHIND
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle); prepositional in the support sense
entries.separable: no — nothing goes between the verb and behind: get behind the candidate, ✗ get the candidate behind.
entries.transitive: either — no object when it means fall behind, an object when it means support
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: falling behind is a change of state (we got behind on the rent in March), and backing somebody is the moment support is thrown (the union got behind the proposal).
entries.passive: no. ✗ the proposal was gotten behind by the union, and the fall behind sense has no object to promote at all.
entries.see also: get ahead, get through, go along with

entries.meaning: Manage — to have just barely enough money, skill, or time to keep going.
examples: They get by on one salary.
My Spanish is bad, but I get by.
We got by for years without a car.
She gets by with a lot of help from her sister.
Nobody in that department is thriving; they're all just getting by.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — get BY
entries.русский: перебиваться, сводить концы с концами; обходиться
entries.separable: not applicable — no object. What you manage on arrives through on or with: get by on one salary, ✗ get one salary by.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; it describes coping over a stretch of time, so the progressive is natural: they're all just getting by, we got by for years without a car.
entries.passive: no — intransitive; what you manage on follows on or with, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ one salary is gotten by on.
entries.see also: get along, get through, go without

entries.meaning: Write something down before you lose it; wear somebody's spirits down; or lower yourself.
examples: Wait — let me get the address down.
I got it down on the back of an envelope.
She got down every word he said.
The gray February weather gets me down.
Don't let them get you down.
Get down — someone's at the window.
He couldn't get down off the ladder by himself.
The band came on and the whole room got down.

senses.head: Write down, record
body: Usually in a hurry: an address, a plate number, a quote. (записать, зафиксировать)
examples: Wait — let me get the address down.
I got it down on the back of an envelope.
She got down every word he said.

senses.head: Depress somebody
body: The subject is the weather, the news, the job. The person always sits between. (угнетать, вгонять в тоску)
examples: The gray February weather gets me down.
Don't let them get you down.

senses.head: Lower yourself, duck
body: No object; often an urgent imperative. (пригнуться, спуститься)
examples: Get down — someone's at the window.
He couldn't get down off the ladder by himself.

senses.head: Dance, let loose
body: Informal and a little dated, out of 1970s American English. (отрываться, зажигать)
examples: The band came on and the whole room got down.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — get it DOWN
entries.separable: yes — get the address down or get down the address, and a pronoun must split: get it down, never ✗ get down it.
entries.transitive: either — an object in the write and depress senses, none in the duck and dance senses
entries.register: everyday — the dancing sense is informal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: recording (let me get the address down), depressing (the gray February weather gets me down), ducking (get down — someone's at the window), and the dated dance sense (the whole room got down).
entries.passive: no in practice. Both transitive senses are causative get, which blocks it: ✗ every word he said was gotten down, ✗ I am gotten down by February. English says don't let them get you down, never a passive.
entries.see also: get down to, get up, get over

entries.meaning: Start giving something your serious attention, after the throat-clearing is over.
examples: Let's get down to business.
It was noon before we got down to any real work.
Once you get down to the details, the plan falls apart.
He can't get down to studying with the television on.
When it gets down to it, they simply don't want to pay.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle down carries the stress and to stays weak — get DOWN tuh business
entries.separable: no — get down to work, ✗ get work down to, ✗ get down work to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; it marks the moment serious attention begins (let's get down to business), and the object is often an -ing form: he can't get down to studying.
entries.passive: no. ✗ business was gotten down to, ✗ no real work was gotten down to before noon.
entries.see also: get around to, get to, get on with

entries.meaning: Arrive; be admitted; or hand something in before the deadline.
examples: The red-eye gets in at 6:15.
We got in after midnight and went straight to bed.
He applied to Michigan and got in.
Get your timesheet in by noon.
I got it in with an hour to spare.
If she gets in, the whole board changes.

senses.head: Arrive
body: Of trains, flights, and people coming home late. (прибывать, приезжать)
examples: The red-eye gets in at 6:15.
We got in after midnight and went straight to bed.

senses.head: Be admitted
body: Of schools, clubs, and anything with a door policy. (поступить, попасть)
examples: He applied to Michigan and got in.

senses.head: Submit something in time
body: Here the object can sit on either side, and a pronoun must sit in front of in. (сдать, подать вовремя)
examples: Get your timesheet in by noon.
I got it in with an hour to spare.

senses.head: Be elected
body: Of candidates and parties; no object. (пройти (на выборах))
examples: If she gets in, the whole board changes.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — get IN; before a place word (get in the car) in is a preposition and leans on the verb
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle); prepositional before a place
entries.separable: yes when in is a particle — get your application in or get in your application, and a pronoun must split: get it in by Friday, never ✗ get in it by Friday. No when in is a preposition of place: you get in the car, and the car can never move in front of in.
entries.transitive: either — no object when it means arrive, an object when you deliver something
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: arriving (the red-eye gets in at 6:15), being admitted (he applied to Michigan and got in), submitting on time (get your timesheet in by noon), and being elected (if she gets in, the whole board changes).
entries.passive: no in ordinary American use. The submit sense is causative: ✗ the timesheet was gotten in by noon — say I got it in with an hour to spare. The other three senses have no object at all.
entries.see also: get in on, get into, get out

entries.meaning: Join something already under way, usually something profitable or fun.
examples: Everybody wants to get in on the deal now that it's working.
He got in on the ground floor of the company.
Ask whether we can get in on the group order.
Four other states have gotten in on it since.
She got in on the joke about a beat late.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle in carries the stress and on stays weak — get IN on it
entries.separable: no — get in on the deal, ✗ get the deal in on, ✗ get in the deal on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: joining something already under way (he got in on the ground floor of the company).
entries.passive: no. ✗ the deal was gotten in on by four other states, ✗ the group order can be gotten in on — the three-part verb has no passive, common though the active is.
entries.see also: get in, get into, go in for

entries.meaning: Become absorbed in something, admitted to something, or tangled up in something.
examples: He got into birding during the pandemic.
I never got into that show.
She got into her first-choice school.
They got into a shouting match in the parking lot.
I don't want to get into the legal side of it tonight.
I don't know what has gotten into him lately.

senses.head: Become interested in, take up
body: The everyday American way to say a hobby has caught you. (увлечься, подсесть на)
examples: He got into birding during the pandemic.
I never got into that show.

senses.head: Be admitted to
body: Of colleges and programs — the transitive twin of get in. (поступить в)
examples: She got into her first-choice school.

senses.head: Become involved in, usually something unwelcome
body: Arguments, trouble, debt, and long topics you would rather skip. (ввязаться в, попасть в)
examples: They got into a shouting match in the parking lot.
I don't want to get into the legal side of it tonight.

senses.head: what has gotten into somebody — explain odd behavior
body: A fixed frame, always with what, about a change nobody can account for. (что на него нашло)
examples: I don't know what has gotten into him lately.

entries.pronunciation note: into is a preposition; the first syllable takes the stress and the second reduces — get INtuh it
entries.separable: no — get into an argument, never ✗ get an argument into.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and inchoative throughout: taking up a hobby (he got into birding during the pandemic), being admitted (she got into her first-choice school), and getting tangled up in something (they got into a shouting match). The fixed what has gotten into him? is frozen in the perfect.
entries.passive: no. ✗ birding was gotten into during the pandemic, ✗ a shouting match was gotten into in the parking lot, ✗ the legal side won't be gotten into tonight.
entries.see also: get in, get out of, get on

entries.meaning: Leave a vehicle, leave work, escape a punishment, or send something on its way.
examples: We get off at the next stop.
She got off the horse without any help.
What time do you get off tonight?
I got off early on Friday.
He got off with a fine and a warning.
A good lawyer got him off.
I need to get this package off before five.
Get the invoices off today if you can.
Get off me — I can stand up on my own.

senses.head: Leave a vehicle; climb down from something
body: Here off is a preposition and the phrase never splits. (сойти, слезть)
examples: We get off at the next stop.
She got off the horse without any help.

senses.head: Finish work
body: No object; the standard American way to ask about someone's shift. (освободиться, закончить работу)
examples: What time do you get off tonight?
I got off early on Friday.

senses.head: Escape punishment — or get somebody else off
body: Intransitive with with; transitive and separable when a lawyer does it for you. (отделаться, выйти сухим из воды)
examples: He got off with a fine and a warning.
A good lawyer got him off.

senses.head: Send something on its way
body: Of letters, packages, and invoices; the object may sit on either side. (отправить, отослать)
examples: I need to get this package off before five.
Get the invoices off today if you can.

senses.head: Get off! — let go, stop touching
body: An imperative, usually with a person or a thing right after it. (отстань, отцепись)
examples: Get off me — I can stand up on my own.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — get it OFF; before a vehicle (get off the bus) off is a preposition and leans on the verb
entries.русский: сойти, выйти (из транспорта); отделаться; отправить; освободиться (с работы)
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle); prepositional before a vehicle or a surface
entries.separable: yes when off is a particle — get the package off or get off a long-overdue letter, and a pronoun must split: get it off in the morning, never ✗ get off it in the morning. No when off is a preposition of place: you get off the bus, and the bus can never move in front of off — ✗ get the bus off.
entries.transitive: either — no object when you leave work, an object when you send something or clear somebody
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: leaving a vehicle (we get off at the next stop), finishing a shift (what time do you get off?), escaping punishment (he got off with a fine), and sending something out (get the invoices off today).
entries.passive: restricted. Only the clear somebody sense really passivizes, and even that is informal: he was gotten off by a good lawyer (Americans prefer the active a good lawyer got him off). ✗ the bus was gotten off at the next stop, ✗ the package was gotten off before five.
entries.see also: get off on, get on, get away with

entries.meaning: Take intense, slightly indecent pleasure in something — often said with disapproval.
examples: He gets off on telling people they're wrong.
She gets off on the pressure of a deadline.
I don't get off on arguing about it the way he does.
They got off on watching the whole thing fall apart.
Some managers really get off on the power.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle off carries the stress and on stays weak — get OFF on it
entries.separable: no — get off on the attention, ✗ get the attention off on.
entries.register: informal — it carries a sexual undertone even when the object is innocent, so it is not a neutral way to say enjoy
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, but close to a verb of feeling, so the habitual present is its home: he gets off on telling people they're wrong, some managers really get off on the power.
entries.passive: no. ✗ the attention is gotten off on, ✗ the pressure of a deadline is gotten off on by her.
entries.see also: get off, go for, go in for

entries.meaning: Board something; make progress; or, of a person or the hour, be getting late.
examples: Get on the bus at Sixth and Elm.
Twenty people got on at the last stop.
How are you getting on with the report?
Her father is getting on — he'll be ninety in May.
It's getting on toward midnight.
That beeping is getting on my nerves.

senses.head: Board
body: Buses, trains, planes, horses, bikes — anything you climb onto rather than into. (садиться (в транспорт))
examples: Get on the bus at Sixth and Elm.
Twenty people got on at the last stop.

senses.head: Make progress with something
body: Usually with with; the American ear hears it as how is it coming along. (продвигаться, справляться)
examples: How are you getting on with the report?

senses.head: be getting on — be growing old, or be growing late
body: Always in the progressive, and always about age or the clock. (стареть; становиться поздно)
examples: Her father is getting on — he'll be ninety in May.
It's getting on toward midnight.

senses.head: get on somebody's nerves — irritate
body: A fixed phrase with nerves, case, or last nerve. (действовать на нервы)
examples: That beeping is getting on my nerves.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — get ON; before a vehicle on is a preposition and leans on the verb
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle); prepositional before a vehicle
entries.separable: no in ordinary use — get on the plane, never ✗ get the plane on. (Putting something onto a surface is the literal get it on the table, a different pattern.)
entries.transitive: either — an object after the preposition, none in be getting on
entries.register: everyday — get on with someone meaning be friendly is British; Americans say get along with
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: boarding (get on the bus at Sixth and Elm) and making progress (how are you getting on with the report?). The growing old / growing late sense exists only in the progressive: her father is getting on, ✗ her father gets on.
entries.passive: no. ✗ the bus was gotten on at the last stop, and the fixed get on somebody's nerves refuses it too: ✗ my nerves are being gotten on by that beeping.
entries.see also: get on with, get off, get along

entries.meaning: Stop stalling and continue with something; in British English, also to be on good terms with somebody.
examples: Let's get on with it — we're forty minutes behind.
He wanted to get on with his life.
Can we get on with the meeting?
In London they ask whether you get on with your flatmates; in Chicago they ask whether you get along with your roommates.
The two of them get on with each other better than anyone expected.

senses.head: Continue with, stop stalling
body: Fully American in this sense — let's get on with it is ordinary speech. (продолжать, приступать)
examples: Let's get on with it — we're forty minutes behind.
He wanted to get on with his life.
Can we get on with the meeting?

senses.head: Have a good relationship with (British)
body: In the US this sense sounds imported; the American verb is get along with. (ладить с)
examples: In London they ask whether you get on with your flatmates; in Chicago they ask whether you get along with your roommates.
The two of them get on with each other better than anyone expected.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle on carries the stress and with stays weak — get ON with it
entries.separable: no — get on with the job, ✗ get the job on with.
entries.register: everyday in the continue sense; the be friendly sense is British, where American English uses get along with
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the American continue sense (let's get on with it — we're forty minutes behind). The British be friendly sense names a relationship rather than an act, but still takes the progressive: they're getting on better than anyone expected.
entries.passive: no. ✗ the job was gotten on with, ✗ the meeting can be gotten on with now.
entries.see also: get along, get on, get down to

entries.meaning: Leave or escape; remove something; or, of news, slip loose.
examples: We got out before the storm hit.
Get out — the alarm is real this time.
She got the stain out with club soda.
I couldn't get it out without breaking the glass.
Word got out that the store was closing.
If this gets out, we're finished.
They got the newsletter out a day late.
You met her? Get out.

senses.head: Leave, escape
body: No object; often an imperative. (выйти, убраться)
examples: We got out before the storm hit.
Get out — the alarm is real this time.

senses.head: Remove something
body: Stains, splinters, dents. The object sits on either side, and a pronoun sits in front. (вывести, вытащить)
examples: She got the stain out with club soda.
I couldn't get it out without breaking the glass.

senses.head: Become known, of news
body: The subject is word, the story, or it; there is no object. (просочиться, стать известным)
examples: Word got out that the store was closing.
If this gets out, we're finished.

senses.head: Produce and release
body: Of newsletters, records, statements — anything you push out the door on a deadline. (выпустить, разослать)
examples: They got the newsletter out a day late.

senses.head: Get out! — disbelief
body: Informal and American, said with the stress on out: you cannot be serious. (да ладно!, не может быть)
examples: You met her? Get out.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — get it OUT
entries.separable: yes — get the splinter out or get out the splinter, and a pronoun must split: get it out, never ✗ get out it.
entries.transitive: either — no object when you leave, an object when you remove or release something
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: leaving (we got out before the storm hit), removing (she got the stain out with club soda), news slipping loose (word got out that the store was closing), and releasing (they got the newsletter out a day late). Get out! as disbelief is a frozen interjection.
entries.passive: restricted at best. The newsletter was gotten out a day late and the stain couldn't be gotten out are heard but stiff; the active is the American default. The leave and become known senses have no object and no passive: ✗ it was gotten out that the store was closing.
entries.see also: get out of, get in, give out

entries.meaning: Wriggle out of a duty, climb out of something, or take something away from an experience.
examples: He got out of jury duty with a doctor's note.
She'll try to get out of going.
Get out of the car slowly and keep your hands visible.
We couldn't get out of the parking garage for an hour.
What do you get out of volunteering there?
I got very little out of that class.
The detectives couldn't get a word out of him.

senses.head: Avoid a duty
body: Jury duty, a shift, a dinner you never wanted to attend. (увильнуть от, отвертеться)
examples: He got out of jury duty with a doctor's note.
She'll try to get out of going.

senses.head: Leave, exit
body: Cars, buildings, bed — anything you climb out of. (выйти из, выбраться из)
examples: Get out of the car slowly and keep your hands visible.
We couldn't get out of the parking garage for an hour.

senses.head: Gain from
body: What an experience is worth to you; the frame is what do you get out of it. (извлечь (пользу), получить от)
examples: What do you get out of volunteering there?
I got very little out of that class.

senses.head: Extract from somebody
body: Here the thing extracted sits right after get. (вытянуть из, добиться от)
examples: The detectives couldn't get a word out of him.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle out carries the stress and of reduces to /əv/ — get OUT uv it
entries.separable: no as a three-part verb — get out of the meeting, ✗ get the meeting out of. Do not confuse it with the separate pattern get something out of somebody, where the object belongs to get and out of introduces a source: get the truth out of him.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: dodging a duty (he got out of jury duty with a doctor's note), exiting (get out of the car slowly), and gaining from an experience (what do you get out of volunteering there?).
entries.passive: no for the three-part verb: ✗ jury duty was gotten out of with a doctor's note, ✗ the parking garage couldn't be gotten out of for an hour. The separate pattern get something out of somebody does passivize, because there the object belongs to plain get: not a word could be gotten out of him.
entries.see also: get out, get away with, get into

entries.meaning: Recover from something that knocked you down, or climb past an obstacle.
examples: It took her a month to get over the flu.
He never really got over the divorce.
We still have to get over the funding problem.
I can't get over my fear of flying.
I can't get over how tall he is.
She still can't get over that they picked her.
We got over the ridge before dark.

senses.head: Recover from
body: Illness, heartbreak, a shock. The object is what hit you. (оправиться от, пережить)
examples: It took her a month to get over the flu.
He never really got over the divorce.

senses.head: Overcome a difficulty
body: Obstacles, fears, and objections rather than injuries. (преодолеть, справиться с)
examples: We still have to get over the funding problem.
I can't get over my fear of flying.

senses.head: can't get over — be amazed
body: Always negative, and about surprise rather than recovery. (не могу поверить, поражаюсь)
examples: I can't get over how tall he is.
She still can't get over that they picked her.

senses.head: Cross
body: The literal sense that the others grew out of: get to the far side. (перебраться через)
examples: We got over the ridge before dark.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on over — get OVer it
entries.separable: no — this is the textbook inseparable one. Get over the flu, never ✗ get the flu over, and a pronoun still follows the whole phrase: get over it, never ✗ get it over. (Get it over with is a different verb — see the next entry.)
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; recovering and overcoming are processes, so the progressive is natural: she's still getting over the flu. The fixed negative can't get over (I can't get over how tall he is) is stative — it reports amazement, not an action.
entries.passive: no. ✗ the flu was finally gotten over, ✗ the funding problem still has to be gotten over, ✗ my fear of flying can't be gotten over. The active is the only option.
entries.see also: get over with, get through, get across

entries.meaning: Finish something unpleasant so that it is finally behind you.
examples: Let's just get it over with.
I want to get the dentist over with before lunch.
She got the hardest chapter over with first.
Can we get this conversation over with?
He'd rather get the whole thing over with today than wait a week.
entries.pronunciation note: over carries the stress and with stays weak — get it Over with
entries.separable: special — this is the one three-part verb on the page that must split. The object goes between get and over: get the exam over with, get it over with. ✗ get over with the exam.
entries.transitive: yes — nearly always a pronoun or a short noun
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: finishing something unpleasant so it is behind you (let's just get it over with, she got the hardest chapter over with first).
entries.passive: no. ✗ the exam was gotten over with before lunch — the frame demands an active with the object wedged between get and over: get the dentist over with.
entries.see also: get over, get through, get down to

entries.meaning: Survive or finish something long; reach somebody by phone; or push a measure past a hurdle.
examples: I don't know how we got through that winter.
She got through the whole reading list in a month.
I called nine times and never got through.
They got the bill through on the last day of the session.
The permit finally got through.
The committee gutted it first, but they got it through.
The four of them got through two pizzas.

senses.head: Finish, survive
body: Of weeks, reading lists, and bad stretches you come out the other side of. (пережить, осилить)
examples: I don't know how we got through that winter.
She got through the whole reading list in a month.

senses.head: Reach somebody by phone
body: No object; the person, if named, arrives through to. (дозвониться)
examples: I called nine times and never got through.

senses.head: Be approved — or push something through
body: Of bills, permits, and applications; transitive and separable here. (пройти, провести (закон))
examples: They got the bill through on the last day of the session.
The permit finally got through.
The committee gutted it first, but they got it through.

senses.head: Consume
body: Slightly informal, about the speed with which supplies vanish. (уйти на, израсходовать)
examples: The four of them got through two pizzas.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on through — get THROUGH it
entries.type: prepositional verb (verb + preposition); a particle when you push something through
entries.separable: usually no — get through the week, and with a pronoun get through it; ✗ get the week through. In the narrow sense of pushing a measure through a body it is separable, and there a pronoun has to split: get the bill through, get it through, ✗ get through it in that meaning.
entries.transitive: either — no object when you reach somebody by phone, an object otherwise
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: surviving a stretch (I don't know how we got through that winter), reaching somebody by phone (I called nine times and never got through), pushing a measure past a hurdle (they got the bill through), and consuming (the four of them got through two pizzas).
entries.passive: restricted. Only the push a measure through sense is anywhere near natural, and even there the plain intransitive wins: the permit finally got through over the permit was finally gotten through. ✗ that winter was gotten through, ✗ two pizzas were gotten through.
entries.see also: get through to, get over, get by

entries.meaning: Make somebody finally understand you; or reach them on the phone.
examples: Nothing I say gets through to him.
She finally got through to the kids about the seatbelts.
If anyone can get through to her, it's you.
I couldn't get through to the billing department.
It took an hour to get through to an actual person.

senses.head: Make somebody understand
body: The object is a person who has not been listening. (достучаться до)
examples: Nothing I say gets through to him.
She finally got through to the kids about the seatbelts.
If anyone can get through to her, it's you.

senses.head: Reach by phone
body: The transitive twin of get through, with the person or department named. (дозвониться до)
examples: I couldn't get through to the billing department.
It took an hour to get through to an actual person.

entries.pronunciation note: through carries the stress and to stays weak — get THROUGH tuh her
entries.separable: no — get through to the kids, ✗ get the kids through to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, making somebody finally understand (nothing I say gets through to him) and reaching them by phone (it took an hour to get through to an actual person).
entries.passive: no. ✗ he is never gotten through to, ✗ the billing department couldn't be gotten through to.
entries.see also: get through, get across, get at

entries.meaning: Reach a place or a point; wear on somebody; or be lucky enough to do something.
examples: We got to Tulsa by three.
I never got to the last chapter.
The noise is starting to get to me.
Don't let him get to you.
I got to meet her at the signing.
The kids get to stay up on Fridays.
They got to talking and lost an hour.

senses.head: Reach a place or a point
body: Physical arrival, or the point you reached in a book or a list. (добраться до, дойти до)
examples: We got to Tulsa by three.
I never got to the last chapter.

senses.head: Wear on somebody, upset them
body: The subject is the noise, the pressure, the person; the object is you. (доставать, задевать)
examples: The noise is starting to get to me.
Don't let him get to you.

senses.head: Have the chance to
body: Followed by a bare verb; the American way to say you were allowed or lucky. (удаваться, посчастливиться)
examples: I got to meet her at the signing.
The kids get to stay up on Fridays.

senses.head: get to talking, get to work — begin
body: Followed by a gerund or a noun, marking the start of an activity. (приняться за, разговориться)
examples: They got to talking and lost an hour.

entries.pronunciation note: to is a preposition and reduces to /tə/, with the stress on the verb — GET tuh me
entries.separable: no — get to the airport, ✗ get the airport to.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: arriving (we got to Tulsa by three) and wearing on somebody (the noise is starting to get to me). The have the chance to sense is a semi-modal — get to plus a bare verb, marking permission or luck (the kids get to stay up on Fridays) — and it has no imperative and no passive.
entries.passive: no. ✗ Tulsa was gotten to by three, ✗ I am being gotten to by the noise, ✗ she was gotten to meet at the signing — none of the four senses passivize.
entries.see also: get around to, get at, get through

entries.meaning: Meet up with people; or gather scattered things into one place.
examples: Let's get together next week.
The four of us got together every Thursday for years.
Can you get the receipts together by Friday?
I got them together in one folder.
He finally got it together and finished the degree.
They got together in college and never split up.

senses.head: Meet socially
body: No object; the people arrive as the subject or through with. (собраться, встретиться)
examples: Let's get together next week.
The four of us got together every Thursday for years.

senses.head: Assemble, gather
body: Papers, money, a team. The object sits on either side of together. (собрать, подготовить)
examples: Can you get the receipts together by Friday?
I got them together in one folder.

senses.head: get it together — pull yourself together
body: Informal, about finally organizing your life or your work. (взять себя в руки, собраться)
examples: He finally got it together and finished the degree.

senses.head: Become a couple
body: No object; of two people starting a relationship. (сойтись, начать встречаться)
examples: They got together in college and never split up.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — get tuhGETHer
entries.separable: yes when there is an object — get the paperwork together or get together the paperwork, and a pronoun splits: get it together, ✗ get together it. When people simply meet, there is no object to place.
entries.transitive: either — no object when people meet, an object when you assemble something
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: meeting (let's get together next week), assembling (can you get the receipts together by Friday?), pulling yourself together (he finally got it together), and pairing off (they got together in college).
entries.passive: no in practice — the assemble sense is causative get: ✗ the receipts were gotten together by Friday, ✗ they were gotten together in one folder. The meet and couple senses take no object at all.
entries.see also: get up, get in on, go out

entries.meaning: Rise from bed or from a chair; or get somebody else on their feet.
examples: I get up at five.
He got up and left without a word.
Could you get me up at six?
She got the whole house up before dawn.
He never got up the nerve to ask her.
The train got up to eighty on the flat stretch.

senses.head: Rise from bed; stand up
body: No object; the plainest sense. (вставать, подниматься)
examples: I get up at five.
He got up and left without a word.

senses.head: Wake or raise somebody
body: The person always sits between the verb and up when it is a pronoun. (будить, поднимать)
examples: Could you get me up at six?
She got the whole house up before dawn.

senses.head: Summon nerve, speed, or steam
body: A fixed set of objects: the nerve, the courage, speed, steam. (набраться (смелости), набрать (скорость))
examples: He never got up the nerve to ask her.
The train got up to eighty on the flat stretch.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — get me UP
entries.separable: yes — get the kids up or get up the kids (rarer), and a pronoun must split: get me up at six, never ✗ get up me.
entries.transitive: either — no object when you rise, an object when you rouse somebody
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: rising (I get up at five), rousing somebody else (could you get me up at six?), and summoning nerve or speed (he never got up the nerve to ask her).
entries.passive: no. ✗ I was gotten up at six, ✗ the whole house was gotten up before dawn, ✗ the nerve was never gotten up — the causative and the fixed-object senses both refuse it.
entries.see also: get up to, get down, get off

entries.meaning: Be doing something, usually something you should not be; or reach a given point in a sequence.
examples: What have those two been getting up to all afternoon?
He got up to all sorts of trouble at boarding school.
We got up to chapter nine before the term ended.
The bidding got up to four thousand.
An American asks what you are up to, not what you are getting up to.

senses.head: Be doing something, usually mischief
body: The British staple. Americans hear it, but rarely say it. (вытворять, натворить)
examples: What have those two been getting up to all afternoon?
He got up to all sorts of trouble at boarding school.

senses.head: Reach a point in a sequence
body: Of chapters, prices, and counts that climb. (дойти до, добраться до)
examples: We got up to chapter nine before the term ended.
The bidding got up to four thousand.

senses.head: Compare with American usage
body: The everyday American frame drops get entirely. (сравните с американским вариантом)
examples: An American asks what you are up to, not what you are getting up to.

entries.pronunciation note: up carries the stress and to stays weak — get UP tuh
entries.separable: no — get up to mischief, ✗ get mischief up to.
entries.register: British — an American would say be up to or get into: What have you been up to?
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: being up to something, usually mischief (what have those two been getting up to?), and reaching a point in a sequence (the bidding got up to four thousand). Chiefly British; the American frame drops get.
entries.passive: no. ✗ all sorts of trouble was gotten up to at boarding school, ✗ chapter nine was gotten up to before the term ended.
entries.see also: get up, get into, go on

entries.meaning: Hand something over for nothing; or let a secret slip.
examples: The church gave away two hundred turkeys.
She gave the whole collection away.
I gave it away to a neighbor.
His face gave him away.
Don't give away the ending.
They gave away a three-goal lead in eleven minutes.
Her uncle gave her away.

senses.head: Hand over for free
body: Of possessions, tickets, food — anything you part with without payment. (раздать, отдать даром)
examples: The church gave away two hundred turkeys.
She gave the whole collection away.
I gave it away to a neighbor.

senses.head: Reveal, betray
body: Of secrets, endings, and the face that will not keep them. (выдать, проболтаться)
examples: His face gave him away.
Don't give away the ending.

senses.head: Lose through carelessness
body: Sports and negotiation: hand the other side an advantage. (упустить, отдать (победу))
examples: They gave away a three-goal lead in eleven minutes.

senses.head: Present the bride
body: The wedding sense, always with a person as the object. (вести к алтарю, отдавать (невесту))
examples: Her uncle gave her away.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — give it aWAY
entries.separable: yes — give the old crib away or give away the old crib, and a pronoun must split: give it away, never ✗ give away it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: donating (the church gave away two hundred turkeys), revealing (his face gave him away), losing an advantage (they gave away a three-goal lead), and presenting the bride (her uncle gave her away).
entries.passive: yes, and it is ordinary in every sense: two hundred turkeys were given away, the ending was given away in the first review, a three-goal lead was given away in eleven minutes, she was given away by her uncle.
entries.see also: give back, give out, give up

entries.meaning: Return what is not yours; or, without an object, put something back into your community.
examples: Give me my keys back.
He gave back every cent he had borrowed.
I'll give it back tomorrow, I promise.
The surgery gave him back his sight.
She wanted a job where she could give back.

senses.head: Return something
body: The plain sense. With two objects the person comes first: give me my keys back. (вернуть, отдать обратно)
examples: Give me my keys back.
He gave back every cent he had borrowed.
I'll give it back tomorrow, I promise.

senses.head: Restore something abstract
body: Of health, sight, confidence — what an event returns to a person. (вернуть (зрение, уверенность))
examples: The surgery gave him back his sight.

senses.head: Contribute to your community
body: No object at all; a warm American idiom of charity and service. (приносить пользу обществу, отдавать долг)
examples: She wanted a job where she could give back.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — give it BACK
entries.separable: yes — give the money back or give back the money, and a pronoun must split: give it back, never ✗ give back it.
entries.transitive: either — an object when you return something, none in the community sense
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: returning an object (give me my keys back), restoring something abstract (the surgery gave him back his sight), and the object-less community sense (she wanted a job where she could give back).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — every cent was given back, his sight was given back to him after the surgery. The community sense is intransitive and has no passive at all.
entries.see also: give away, get back, give up

entries.meaning: Stop resisting — surrender an argument, a demand, or a craving.
examples: After two hours of arguing he gave in.
Neither side would give in.
I gave in to the craving and bought the donuts.
Don't give in to him just to end the fight.
The company refused to give in to the strikers.

senses.head: Stop resisting
body: No object; the end of a standoff. (уступить, сдаться)
examples: After two hours of arguing he gave in.
Neither side would give in.

senses.head: give in to — yield to a feeling or a demand
body: The object arrives through to: temptation, pressure, a bully. (поддаться, уступить (чему-то))
examples: I gave in to the craving and bought the donuts.
Don't give in to him just to end the fight.
The company refused to give in to the strikers.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — give IN
entries.separable: not applicable in American use — give in takes no object, and what you yield to arrives through to: give in to the pressure, give in to it; ✗ give the pressure in. (In the British hand in sense it does take an object and does split: give your essay in, give it in.)
entries.transitive: no — intransitive; the thing you yield to follows to
entries.register: everyday — British English also uses give in for handing in schoolwork, where Americans say hand in or turn in
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; it names the moment resistance ends (after two hours of arguing he gave in), and give in to covers yielding to a feeling or a demand (I gave in to the craving).
entries.passive: no — intransitive in American use, so there is nothing to promote. The prepositional passive is marginal at best (?their demands were finally given in to), and ✗ the craving was given in to is not what anyone says.
entries.see also: give up, give over, go along with

entries.meaning: Send out heat, light, or a smell — or, informally, an impression.
examples: The heater gives off a burning smell for the first minute.
Those bulbs give off almost no heat.
The marsh gave off a sour smell after the rain.
He gives off the impression that he'd rather be somewhere else.
The whole place gave off a summer-camp feeling.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — give OFF a smell
entries.separable: no in practice — the object follows the whole phrase: give off a strange smell. ✗ give a strange smell off, and ✗ give it off sounds wrong to most American ears, which is unusual for a particle verb.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic emission of heat, light, or smell (the heater gives off a burning smell for the first minute), though with a permanent property it reads almost statively: those bulbs give off almost no heat. The informal impression sense is the same pattern applied to people.
entries.passive: restricted. Natural in scientific and technical writing — heat is given off during the reaction — but stilted in everyday use (?a sour smell was given off by the marsh), and the impression sense refuses it: ✗ the impression that he'd rather be elsewhere is given off by him.
entries.see also: give out, give away, go off

entries.meaning: Of a window, a door, or a room: open toward something, look out on it.
examples: The kitchen window gives onto a small courtyard.
Both bedrooms give onto the garden.
A narrow door gave onto the stairwell.
The terrace gives onto the harbor and catches the evening light.
An American listing would say the room opens onto the patio rather than gives onto it.
entries.pronunciation note: onto is a preposition; the stress sits on its first syllable — give ONtuh the garden
entries.separable: no — give onto the courtyard, ✗ give the courtyard onto.
entries.register: formal — chiefly British and literary; American listings say look out on or open onto
entries.verb type: stative — a fixed property of a window, a door, or a room rather than anything done: both bedrooms give onto the garden. It rejects the progressive: ✗ both bedrooms are giving onto the garden.
entries.passive: no. Like other stative verbs it refuses the passive even though it always takes an object: ✗ the garden is given onto by both bedrooms, ✗ a small courtyard is given onto by the kitchen window.
entries.see also: give off, give out, go out

entries.meaning: Hand things out to a crowd; or, of a body part or a machine, quit working.
examples: Volunteers gave out water at mile six.
She gave the tests out face down.
I gave them out in the hallway after class.
His knees gave out on the last flight of stairs.
The generator gave out around midnight.
Our water gave out on the second day.
They won't give out customer numbers over the phone.

senses.head: Distribute
body: Of flyers, water, tests — anything handed around to many people. (раздавать)
examples: Volunteers gave out water at mile six.
She gave the tests out face down.
I gave them out in the hallway after class.

senses.head: Stop working, fail
body: Of knees, voices, engines, generators. No object. (отказать, сдать)
examples: His knees gave out on the last flight of stairs.
The generator gave out around midnight.

senses.head: Run out, be exhausted
body: Of supplies: the subject is what ran out. (иссякнуть, закончиться)
examples: Our water gave out on the second day.

senses.head: Release information
body: Of numbers, names, addresses — usually in the negative. (разглашать, сообщать)
examples: They won't give out customer numbers over the phone.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — give them OUT
entries.separable: yes in the distribute sense — give the flyers out or give out the flyers, and a pronoun splits: give them out, ✗ give out them. In the fail sense there is no object at all.
entries.transitive: either — an object when you distribute, none when something fails
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: distributing (volunteers gave out water at mile six), failing (his knees gave out on the last flight of stairs), running out (our water gave out on the second day), and releasing information (they won't give out customer numbers).
entries.passive: restricted — yes in the distribute and release senses: water was given out at mile six, customer numbers are not given out over the phone. No in the fail and run out senses, which are intransitive: ✗ his knees were given out, ✗ our water was given out on the second day.
entries.see also: give away, give up, give in

entries.meaning: Hand something into somebody else's control, or devote a space or a stretch of time entirely to one purpose.
examples: He gave the business over to his daughter.
They gave it over to the county in 1974.
The whole basement is given over to storage.
Most of the hour was given over to questions.
In Yorkshire you may hear give over, where an American would say knock it off.

senses.head: Hand over, surrender control of
body: Of businesses, land, and duties passed to another party. (передать, отдать)
examples: He gave the business over to his daughter.
They gave it over to the county in 1974.

senses.head: Devote entirely to
body: Almost always passive: a room, an hour, a chapter given over to one use. (отвести под, посвятить)
examples: The whole basement is given over to storage.
Most of the hour was given over to questions.

senses.head: give over! — stop it (British)
body: A Northern English imperative with no American currency. (прекрати!, хватит!)
examples: In Yorkshire you may hear give over, where an American would say knock it off.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — give it Over
entries.separable: yes — give the files over to the auditors or give over the files, and a pronoun splits: give them over, ✗ give over them.
entries.transitive: yes — most often in the passive, be given over to
entries.register: formal — the British exclamation give over! (= stop it) is not used in America
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: handing control to somebody (he gave the business over to his daughter) and devoting a space or a stretch of time to a single use (the basement is given over to storage). The British imperative give over! is frozen and has no American currency.
entries.passive: yes — and the devote sense practically lives in the passive: the whole basement is given over to storage, most of the hour was given over to questions. The surrender sense passivizes too: the land was given over to the county in 1974.
entries.see also: give up, give away, give in

entries.meaning: Stop trying; quit a habit; or hand over something you would rather keep.
examples: Don't give up now — you're two pages from the end.
After four rejections he gave up.
She gave up smoking in 2019.
I've given coffee up twice and gone back both times.
He gave his seat up to an older woman.
They had to give it up when the lease ended.
He gave himself up at the county line.
Give it up for the band.

senses.head: Stop trying
body: No object; the most common sense of all. (сдаться, опустить руки)
examples: Don't give up now — you're two pages from the end.
After four rejections he gave up.

senses.head: Quit a habit
body: Followed by a noun or an -ing form: smoking, coffee, biting your nails. (бросить (привычку))
examples: She gave up smoking in 2019.
I've given coffee up twice and gone back both times.

senses.head: Surrender something you have
body: Seats, claims, time, a weekend — the object may sit on either side. (уступить, отдать)
examples: He gave his seat up to an older woman.
They had to give it up when the lease ended.

senses.head: Turn yourself or somebody in
body: Of suspects surrendering to the police. (сдаться (полиции), выдать)
examples: He gave himself up at the county line.

senses.head: give it up for — applaud
body: Informal and American, from stages and comedy clubs. (поаплодируем!)
examples: Give it up for the band.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — give it UP
entries.separable: yes — give your seat up or give up your seat, and a pronoun must split: give it up, never ✗ give up it. With no object (don't give up) there is nothing to place.
entries.transitive: either — no object when you stop trying, an object when you surrender something
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all five senses (quitting, surrendering a seat, turning yourself in); the applause formula Give it up for the band is a fixed imperative, not a separate class
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the habit was given up in 2019, his seat was given up to an older woman, the weapons were given up at the county line. None for the intransitive don't give up, and the reflexive resists it: ✗ he was given up by himself.
entries.see also: give up on, give in, get over

entries.meaning: Stop believing that somebody or something will ever come through.
examples: Her teachers had given up on her by tenth grade.
Don't give up on the car yet — it may just be the starter.
I gave up on the book halfway through.
They never gave up on him, not once.
We had given up on ever hearing back from the agency.
entries.pronunciation note: up carries the stress and on stays weak — give UP on him
entries.separable: no — give up on the car, ✗ give the car up on. Note the contrast with plain give up, which does split: give the car up.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, but it names a change of attitude rather than an act, so the progressive is limited to I'm giving up on this
entries.passive: restricted — the prepositional passive works best with no agent: by tenth grade she had been given up on. With a by-phrase it turns clumsy: ?she was given up on by her teachers.
entries.see also: give up, give in, get over

entries.meaning: Tackle a task in a particular way, or simply carry on with what you normally do.
examples: There's a right way and a wrong way to go about this.
How would you go about finding a plumber out here?
People went about their business as if nothing had happened.
He goes about his day on a fixed schedule.
A rumor went about that the plant would close — in the US it would have gone around.

senses.head: Tackle a task in a given way
body: Usually with it or an -ing form, and often in a question about method. (приниматься за, подходить к (делу))
examples: There's a right way and a wrong way to go about this.
How would you go about finding a plumber out here?

senses.head: Carry on with your routine
body: Nearly always with business, day, or work. (заниматься (своими делами))
examples: People went about their business as if nothing had happened.
He goes about his day on a fixed schedule.

senses.head: Circulate, of rumors (British)
body: Americans say go around here. (ходить (о слухах))
examples: A rumor went about that the plant would close — in the US it would have gone around.

entries.pronunciation note: about is a preposition here and leans on the verb, but in the fixed go about it the stress lands on about
entries.русский: приниматься за, браться (как-то делать); заниматься своим делом
entries.separable: no — go about the repair, ✗ go the repair about.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both American senses: tackling a task a certain way, and carrying on with your routine
entries.passive: no — go stays intransitive and the object belongs to the preposition: ✗ the repair was gone about the wrong way, ✗ their business was gone about as usual.
entries.see also: go around, go at, go into

entries.meaning: Chase somebody or something — a runner, a job, a record, a reputation.
examples: The dog went after a squirrel and took the leash with him.
She's going after the manager's job.
He went after the record all season.
The paper went after the mayor for weeks.
Their attorney went after the witness hard.

senses.head: Chase
body: The literal sense: pursue on foot or in a car. (гнаться за, броситься за)
examples: The dog went after a squirrel and took the leash with him.

senses.head: Try hard to get
body: Of jobs, records, contracts, and titles. (добиваться, идти за)
examples: She's going after the manager's job.
He went after the record all season.

senses.head: Attack or criticize
body: Of prosecutors, reporters, and opponents. (нападать на, обрушиться на)
examples: The paper went after the mayor for weeks.
Their attorney went after the witness hard.

entries.pronunciation note: after is a preposition, so the verb keeps the main stress — GO after him
entries.русский: гнаться за, преследовать; добиваться; наброситься на
entries.separable: no — go after the job, never ✗ go the job after.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses (chase on foot, pursue a job or a record, attack in print)
entries.passive: no — the object sits behind a preposition and will not front: ✗ the mayor was gone after for weeks, ✗ the record was gone after all season.
entries.see also: go at, go for, get back at

entries.meaning: Act contrary to something, or turn out badly for somebody.
examples: It goes against everything she believes.
He went against his father's advice and enlisted.
If the vote goes against us, we appeal.
The ruling went against the tenants.
Nothing in the report goes against what the inspector found.

senses.head: Oppose, act contrary to
body: Of advice, principles, orders, and the grain of your own beliefs. (идти против, противоречить)
examples: It goes against everything she believes.
He went against his father's advice and enlisted.

senses.head: Turn out unfavorably for
body: Of votes, rulings, and decisions; the loser is the object. (сложиться не в пользу)
examples: If the vote goes against us, we appeal.
The ruling went against the tenants.

senses.head: Contradict the evidence
body: A quieter sense: to be inconsistent with what is known. (расходиться с, противоречить)
examples: Nothing in the report goes against what the inspector found.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on against — go aGAINST it
entries.русский: идти против, противоречить; сложиться не в пользу
entries.separable: no — go against the rules, ✗ go the rules against.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic when you defy something (he went against his father's advice); closer to stative in it goes against everything she believes and nothing in the report goes against the findings, where the progressive is odd: ✗ it is going against everything she believes
entries.passive: no — ✗ his father's advice was gone against, ✗ the tenants were gone against by the ruling. Say the ruling favored the landlord instead.
entries.see also: go along with, go for, go by

entries.meaning: Start or continue — and, as an invitation, please do.
examples: Go ahead — I'm listening.
They went ahead without waiting for approval.
The wedding went ahead despite the storm.
The merger will go ahead in April.
We decided to go ahead with the renovation.

senses.head: Proceed; please proceed
body: Often a one-word permission: go ahead. (давай, приступай)
examples: Go ahead — I'm listening.
They went ahead without waiting for approval.

senses.head: Happen as planned
body: Of events that might have been called off. (состояться)
examples: The wedding went ahead despite the storm.
The merger will go ahead in April.

senses.head: go ahead with — carry out
body: The transitive frame, with the plan after with. (приступить к, осуществить)
examples: We decided to go ahead with the renovation.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — go aHEAD
entries.separable: not applicable — no object. What proceeds arrives through with: go ahead with the plan, ✗ go the plan ahead.
entries.transitive: no — intransitive; go ahead with takes its object through the preposition
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the bare Go ahead is the same dynamic verb used as an imperative granting permission
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ the wedding was gone ahead, and go ahead with keeps its object behind the preposition: ✗ the renovation was gone ahead with.
entries.see also: go on, go through with, go for

entries.meaning: Move forward as things develop, or tag along with somebody.
examples: I'll explain as we go along.
He made the rules up as he went along.
The work got easier as we went along.
She went along to keep him company.
Can I go along?

senses.head: Proceed, as you go
body: Almost always in as we go along: learning or deciding on the fly. (по ходу дела, постепенно)
examples: I'll explain as we go along.
He made the rules up as he went along.
The work got easier as we went along.

senses.head: Accompany somebody
body: No object; the person you join is the subject's company. (пойти вместе, сопровождать)
examples: She went along to keep him company.
Can I go along?

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — go aLONG
entries.русский: продвигаться, по ходу дела; пойти вместе
entries.separable: not applicable — no object; a companion arrives through with.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; sense 1 lives almost entirely inside the adverbial as we go along, sense 2 means tagging along with someone
entries.passive: no — intransitive in both senses: ✗ the rules were made up as they were gone along, ✗ he was gone along with to keep him company.
entries.see also: go along with, go on, go with

entries.meaning: Accept somebody else's plan or story, whether or not you like it.
examples: I'll go along with whatever the group decides.
She didn't like the plan but went along with it.
Don't just go along with him to keep the peace.
The board went along with the recommendation.
He went along with the joke for about ten seconds.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle along carries the stress and with stays weak — go aLONG with it
entries.separable: no — go along with the plan, ✗ go the plan along with.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; it reports a decision to accept, so the progressive is uncommon outside I'm going along with it for now
entries.passive: no — ✗ the recommendation was gone along with by the board. American English says the recommendation was accepted.
entries.see also: go against, give in, go for

entries.meaning: Be enough for everyone; circulate; or take the long way past something.
examples: There aren't enough chairs to go around.
Something is going around the office.
A story went around that they'd sold the farm.
You can't go around telling people that.
The bridge was out, so we had to go around.

senses.head: Be enough for everyone
body: Always with enough … to go around. (хватить на всех)
